note: IF Academy original content carried over from the first Advanced Plus course (app/courses/ef-c2.js): grammar explanations and exercises for 16 units, and 8 listening scripts.

1A.rule:
At C2, will, would and should do much more than talk about the future.

will — typical behaviour, annoying habitsShe will sit for hours without saying a word. · He will keep interrupting! (stressed = irritation)
will — deduction about nowThat'll be the courier. (I'm fairly sure)
would — past habits, past refusalAs a child I would read under the covers. · The car wouldn't start.
would — softening opinionsI would imagine / I'd say it's too late.
should — expectation, probabilityThe results should be out by Friday.
should — after if/in case (formal), subjunctive useShould you need help, call me. · It's vital that he should be told.

ex.q: My flatmate ___ leave the lights on — it drives me mad!
ex.why: Stressed will = an irritating habit now.

ex.q: When we were kids, Dad ___ take us fishing every Sunday.
Someone at the door? That ___ be Aidos — he said he'd come at six.
___ you require further information, do not hesitate to contact us.
I ___ say that the plan is a little ambitious. (polite opinion)

ex.a: The parcel should arrive by the end of the week.

1B.rule:
Advanced writing packs a lot of information into the noun phrase.

compound nounsa parenting style, screen-time limits
noun + preposition phrasea fear of failure, the role of grandparents
noun + participlechildren raised abroad, parents working long hours
noun + to-infinitivethe decision to move, an attempt to help
possessive 's vs ofthe children's needs (people) · the end of the film (things)
hyphenated compound adjectivesa ten-year-old boy, a well-meaning parent

ex.q: Choose the most natural noun phrase.
o: a boy who is ten years old

ex.q: Parents ___ long hours often feel guilty.
Choose the correct form.
ex.why: For things, of is usually more natural.

ex.q: Her decision ___ (leave) the company surprised everyone.
Children ___ in two languages often code-switch.

ex.a: The role of grandparents is often overlooked.

2A.g: Modal verbs (2): can, could, be able to, may, might
2A.rule:
can / could — ability, general possibilityStress can affect your sleep. · It could get cold at night.
was able to / managed to — a specific past successThe climbers were able to reach the summit. (not could)
couldn't — past inability (general or specific)We couldn't find a way down.
may / might / could have + past participle — speculation about the pastShe might have missed the bus.
could have — unrealised possibility, criticismYou could have told me!
may well / might well / could well — strong likelihoodPrices may well rise again.
might as well — no better alternativeThe last bus has gone; we might as well walk.

ex.q: After six hours, the rescuers ___ reach the injured climber.
ex.why: A specific past success: was/were able to or managed to.

ex.q: You ___ have warned me about the exam — I had no idea!
There's nothing on TV. We ___ as well go to bed.
She isn't answering. She ___ have left her phone at home. (possibility)
Inflation ___ well rise again next year.

ex.a: They managed to finish the race despite the injury.

2B.rule:
Participle clauses add information concisely, especially in narratives. The subject is usually the same as in the main clause.

-ing — actions at the same time / reasonWalking along the ridge, we saw an eagle. · Feeling exhausted, he stopped.
having + past participle — an earlier actionHaving crossed the desert, they rested for a week.
past participle — passive meaningExhausted by the climb, she fell asleep.
after conjunctionsBefore setting off, check the weather. · When asked, he refused.
reduced relativesThe path leading to the lake was closed.

ex.q: ___ the summit, they took photos and started down.
___ by the storm, the hikers sheltered in a cave.
Before ___ (set) off, make sure your phone is charged.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Walking to the station, it started to rain.
Walking to the station, I got caught in the rain.

ex.q: The road ___ to the village was blocked by snow.

ex.a: Having lost the map, they followed the river.

3A.rule:
zero article — general plural/uncountableOlder people tend to sleep less. · Research shows…
the + adjective — groupsthe elderly, the young, the unemployed
a / an with uncountables in a specific sensea good education, a knowledge of history
quantifiers + of + the/possessivemost of the participants, none of my friends
few / a few, little / a littleFew people knew (= almost none). · A few people knew (= some).
every / each, either / neitherEach participant was tested. · Neither result was significant.

ex.q: ___ elderly are often more satisfied with life than young adults.
___ research suggests that happiness rises after fifty.
Very ___ people realised the study had been flawed. (almost none)
___ of the two groups showed any improvement. (not one, not the other)
She has ___ excellent knowledge of statistics.

ex.a: Most of the participants were over sixty.

3B.rule:
fronting for emphasisStrange it may seem, but it's true. · This I cannot accept.
inversion after negative adverbialsNever had the audience heard such language.
object + particle with pronounsTurn it off. (not turn off it)
adverbs of frequency with modal/auxHe has always loved Shakespeare.
long objects moved to the endShe explained to the class what the play was really about.
indirect questionsDo you know what time it starts? (not what time does it start)

ex.q: Choose the correct order.
o: Can you tell me where is the theatre?
Can you tell me where the theatre is?

ex.q: Choose the correct sentence.
Rarely ___ a play so moving.
She has ___ (always / admire) his sonnets.
Choose the more natural sentence.
o: He explained what the soliloquy meant to us.
He explained to us what the soliloquy meant.

ex.a: Never had the audience heard such language.

4A.rule:
verbsToy marketing leads to / results in / gives rise to stereotypes. · Stereotypes stem from / arise from early experiences.
nounsThe root cause of… · a consequence of… · has an impact on…
linkersOwing to / due to + noun · consequently, as a result, thereby + -ing
trigger / bring about / promptThe report prompted a debate. · The law brought about real change.

Note: result in (cause → effect) but result from (effect ← cause).

ex.q: Gender stereotypes often stem ___ the toys children play with.
The campaign resulted ___ a 20% rise in applications.
The match was cancelled ___ to heavy rain.
The new policy ___ about a major change in hiring.
They lowered prices, ___ attracting new customers.

ex.a: The report prompted a national debate.

4B.rule:
Perfect aspect looks back from a point (completion, result, time up to now). Continuous aspect shows activity in progress, duration or temporariness.

present perfect simple — result, numberI've answered forty emails today.
present perfect continuous — activity, durationI've been answering emails all morning.
past perfect continuous — background durationShe had been working there for years when she quit.
future perfect / future continuousBy 2030 I'll have paid off the loan. · This time tomorrow I'll be flying.
stative verbs rarely continuousI've known him for years. (not been knowing)

ex.q: I'm exhausted — I ___ all day.
She ___ three reports this week.
By the end of the year, we ___ (open) five new offices.
They ___ each other since university.
He ___ overtime for months before he burnt out.

ex.a: This time next week I will be lying on a beach.

5A.rule:
adjective + prepositionapprehensive about, resentful of, indifferent to, overwhelmed by
verb + object + prepositionShe accused him of lying. · They congratulated us on winning.
preposition + -ingShe left without saying goodbye. · Instead of complaining, act.
prepositions at the end of clausesThat's the film I told you about. · What are you worried about?
it + adjective + that / toIt's only natural to feel nervous.

ex.q: She was apprehensive ___ moving abroad.
He seemed completely indifferent ___ the news.
They accused the manager ___ ignoring complaints.
She left the room without ___ a word.
What are you so anxious ___?

ex.a: It is only natural to feel nervous before an exam.

5B.g: Advanced structures for comparing and contrasting
5B.rule:
the … the …The longer you live abroad, the more you notice home.
modifiersconsiderably / far / a great deal more formal · nowhere near as polite · not nearly as direct
contrast linkerswhereas / while + clause · unlike + noun · as opposed to · by contrast
concessionMuch as I love Italy, … · Although / Even though … · Despite / In spite of + -ing / noun
similaritySimilarly, … · likewise · just as … so …

ex.q: ___ more you travel, the more tolerant you become.
British English is ___ near as direct as Dutch.
___ the British, Kazakhs often greet everyone in the room.
___ I admire their punctuality, I find it a little rigid.
In Japan, bowing is common, ___ in Russia people usually shake hands.

ex.a: The longer you stay, the harder it is to leave.

6A.rule:
front (comment / linking)Surprisingly, the old phone outlasted the new one. · However, …
mid (frequency, certainty, focus)She rarely uses apps. · They have probably left. · He even repairs his own laptop.
end (manner, place, time)He fixed it carefully in the garage last night. (manner → place → time)
never between verb and objectShe speaks English fluently. (not speaks fluently English)
meaning can changeOnly I saw it. · I only saw it. · I saw only it.

ex.q: Choose the correct sentence.
He has ___ forgotten to back up his files. (frequency)
Choose the correct order.
o: He repaired it last night carefully.
He repaired it carefully last night.

ex.q: ___, the old typewriter still works. (It is surprising)
They will ___ have arrived by now.

ex.a: She rarely checks her phone in the evening.

6B.rule:
collective nouns (BrE)The team is / are training. (singular = unit; plural = members)
always pluralThe police are… · People were… · Cattle graze…
uncountable, look pluralThe news is… · Mathematics is… · Economics is…
amounts as one unitTen kilometres is a long way. · Five thousand tenge isn't much.
a number of / the number ofA number of students are… · The number of students is…
each / every / neither / noneEach of the answers is correct. · None of us is / are sure (both used).

ex.q: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
The police ___ investigating the accident.
Twenty minutes ___ not long to wait.
The number of users ___ (have) doubled.
A number of people ___ complained.

ex.a: Each of the answers is worth two points.

7A.rule:
reporting passivesThe suspect is said to have fled abroad. · It is believed that …
passive infinitivesHe expects to be released soon. · She hates being told what to do.
perfect / continuous passivesThe case has been reopened. · The witness is being questioned.
modal passivesIt can't have been stolen — the door was locked.
have / get something doneThey had the locks changed. · He got his car broken into.

ex.q: The thief is thought ___ through the window.
The witness ___ by the police at the moment.
The painting can't ___ (steal) — it's still on the wall.
We had our house ___ last year.
She hates ___ what to do.

ex.a: The case is expected to be closed next month.

7B.rule:
past tenses for distance / politenessI was wondering if you could help. · I wanted to ask you something.
past for unreal presentIt's time we left. · I'd rather you didn't tell anyone. · If only I had more time.
present for narratives, jokes, headlinesSo this man walks into a café… · Hermit leaves cave after 30 years.
present simple for timetablesThe film starts at eight.
future in the pastI was going to call you, but… · We knew it would be hard.

ex.q: It's high time we ___ home.
I ___ wondering if you could lend me your notes.
I'd rather you ___ (not / mention) it to anyone.
Headline: "Local woman ___ lottery twice"
I ___ phone you, but my battery died.

ex.a: If only I had more time to read.

8A.rule:
alternatives to ifprovided / providing (that), as long as, on condition that, unless, supposing, otherwise
inversion (formal)Had I known, I'd have come. · Were it not for her, … · Should you need help, …
but for / if it weren't forBut for the recipe, the dish would have failed.
mixed conditionalsIf I'd trained as a chef, I'd be running a restaurant now.
even if / only ifI wouldn't eat it even if you paid me. · Only if it's fresh will I buy it.

ex.q: ___ I known you were vegetarian, I'd have cooked something else.
You can borrow my car ___ you return it by six.
___ it not for her help, we would have failed.
___ the rain, the picnic would have been perfect.
I wouldn't eat insects ___ you paid me.

ex.a: Only if the fish is fresh will I buy it.

8B.rule:
Before a noun, adjectives usually follow this order (you rarely need more than three):

opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose → NOUN

examplea beautiful small antique round Persian silk rug
more naturala lovely old wooden table · huge black boots
commasbetween adjectives of the same type: a cheerful, friendly waiter
after the noun / verbThe view was breathtaking. · something unusual

ex.q: Choose the correct order.
Choose the correct order.
Choose the correct order.
I saw something ___ (strange) on the way home.
Choose the correct order.

ex.a: She bought a beautiful old Italian painting.

1A.title: A coach on what really motivates us
1A.intro: A podcast interview with a performance coach.

script.t: You've coached athletes and executives. What separates people who keep going from those who give up?
Honestly? It's rarely talent. People who last tend to have a reason that's bigger than the result — they'll train in the rain because they love the process, not the medal.
So rewards don't work?

They work for routine tasks. But for anything creative, research suggests that big external rewards can actually reduce motivation. People start doing it for the prize, and when the prize goes, so does the drive.
What would you say to a student who's lost interest in English, say?
I'd ask them to find a small win every day — one film scene understood, one conversation without switching languages. Progress you can see is the most underrated motivator there is.

ex.q: According to the coach, people who keep going usually…
o: have a deeper reason than the result

ex.q: When do external rewards work well?
The coach thinks big prizes always increase motivation.
What does he recommend for a demotivated student?

2B.title: A cyclist's journey across Central Asia
2B.intro: A traveller describes the hardest day of her trip.

script.t: You cycled from Almaty to Istanbul. What was the toughest moment?
Day forty, in the desert. My back wheel broke, and having been warned there were no villages for eighty kilometres, I panicked.
What did you do?
I pushed the bike — well, trudged, really — for six hours. Then a truck driver stopped. He couldn't speak English and I couldn't speak Turkmen, but we were able to fix the wheel together with wire.
Would you do it again?
Absolutely. I might well have given up that day if he hadn't stopped. But that's what I learnt: you can't plan everything — sometimes strangers are the plan.

ex.q: What happened on day forty?
How did she move for six hours?
Elena and the driver had a language in common.
What lesson did she learn?
o: Strangers can be part of the solution.

3A.title: Do we really get happier with age?
3A.intro: Two researchers discuss a study on a radio science programme.

script.t: Your study claims people become happier after their fifties. How big was the sample?
Just over forty thousand adults in twelve countries, followed for ten years. The pattern is a U-shape: satisfaction dips in middle age and rises again.
Some critics say the finding is flawed — that unhappy people simply die earlier.
That's a fair point, and we did control for health. The correlation remained significant even among people in good health.
So what explains it?
We can't be certain — correlation isn't causation. But a likely factor is expectations: older people tend to compare themselves less with others.

ex.q: How many adults were in the study?
What shape describes the pattern?
The researcher completely rejects the critics' point.
What factor does he suggest?

4B.title: Can a four-day week work?
4B.intro: A manager and an employee discuss a trial at their company.

script.t: So, six months into the four-day-week trial — what's the verdict from HR?
By and large, positive. Productivity hasn't dropped; in fact our main KPI, customer satisfaction, has gone up slightly.
And sick days?
Down by almost a third. People have been coming in rested. The cons? Some clients expect replies on Fridays, so we've had to rota a small team.
Will the CEO make it permanent?
The board meets in March — that's TBC. But I'd be surprised if they reversed it. Staff turnover has fallen too, which saves a fortune in recruitment.

ex.q: What happened to productivity?
o: It stayed the same or improved.

ex.q: By how much did sick days fall?
What was one disadvantage?
The decision to make it permanent has already been made.

5B.title: Culture shock in reverse
5B.intro: Two people discuss coming home after years abroad.

script.t: Everyone warns you about culture shock abroad. Nobody warned me about coming home.
Reverse culture shock! I felt it after Spain. The longer I'd been away, the stranger everything seemed — even queuing.
Exactly. In London people apologise constantly, whereas here we're more direct. At first I found it almost rude — my own culture!
And friends weren't nearly as interested in my stories as I expected. That made me feel quite resentful, honestly.
Much as I love being back, I miss being anonymous. Here everyone knows your business.
It took me about a year to feel content again. You end up somewhere in between — not fully either.

ex.q: What surprised Arman?
How does Arman compare London and home?
o: People at home are more direct.

ex.q: Why did Sofia feel resentful?
o: Friends weren't very interested in her stories.

ex.q: Sofia felt completely settled within a month.

6B.title: When maths goes wrong
6B.intro: A science podcast about famous number mistakes.

script.t: Today: tiny numbers, huge consequences. Daniel, you collect maths mistakes.
I do! My favourite is a bridge that was built from both banks at once. One side used a reference height that differed by about half a metre, and the error was doubled instead of corrected.
So the two halves didn't meet?
Not at first — they were nearly a metre apart. Then there's the case of a medicine dose where a decimal point was in the wrong place: ten times the amount.
Frightening. What's the lesson?
Mathematics is rarely the problem; communication is. A number of disasters happen because two teams each assume the other has checked.

ex.q: What went wrong with the bridge?
How far apart were the halves at first?
What caused the medicine error?
o: a decimal point in the wrong place

ex.q: Daniel thinks most disasters are caused by bad maths.

7A.title: A true-crime podcast
7A.intro: Two hosts discuss an unsolved museum theft.

script.t: So, the painting vanished from the gallery overnight. No alarm, no broken glass.
Which is why the police think it must have been taken by someone with a key. The night guard was questioned for hours.
And released without charge. It's now believed that the frame had been replaced weeks earlier with a copy.
Meaning the original might already have been sold before anyone noticed. If it's ever recovered, the thief is expected to face at least ten years.
Unless he's acquitted. The defence will argue that nobody can prove when the swap happened.
It's time we heard from our listeners — who do you think did it?

ex.q: How did the thief probably get in?
The night guard was charged with the crime.
What is now believed?
o: The painting was a copy all along.
A copy had replaced the original weeks earlier.

ex.q: What will the defence argue?
o: Nobody can prove when the swap happened.

8A.title: Love at first bite
8A.intro: A chef and a food writer talk about food and relationships.

script.t: They say the way to someone's heart is through their stomach. As a chef, do you believe it?
Provided the cooking is honest, yes. The first meal I made for my wife was a disaster — I burnt the rice. But for her sense of humour, we'd never have had a second date.
So it wasn't the food that won her over!
Not that night. But food is about attention. If you notice someone sipping their tea slowly, savouring it, you learn what they love.
And acquired tastes?
Ah — she couldn't stand kumis when we met. Had you told me she'd be drinking it every morning ten years later, I wouldn't have believed you.

ex.q: What went wrong at the first meal?
Why was there a second date?
According to the chef, food is about…
His wife loved kumis from the start.
